strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates the limitation of static full-series encoding and proposes adaptive segment selection as a natural solution
Technically sound hierarchical RL approach with asymmetric optimization for controller (trajectory-level) and reasoner (final-round), well-justified for the task structure
Comprehensive evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (clinical, financial, environmental, general) with broad baseline coverage (text LLMs, domain-specific, vision-language models)
Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) demonstrating each component's contribution; reliability reward shows 21.44% impact when removed
Insightful data utilization analysis (Figure 3) showing accuracy peaks at 30-70% coverage, providing evidence for selective processing benefit
Extensive reproducibility details: prompts, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and SFT curation procedures in appendices
Clever reliability-based reward (Eq. 8) using answer consistency under repeated sampling to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky correct outputs
weaknesses: Unclear necessity of adaptive selection: Figure 3 doesn't prove that adaptive (reasoning-based) selection outperforms static segment sampling at 30-70% coverage; simpler approaches may achieve similar results

Imbalanced contribution: SFT alone provides 5.65 average accuracy points (~75% of total 6.46 gain), while RL adds only 1.81 points, raising questions about whether RL's adaptive selection is the primary driver

Anomalous Sleep-QA results: ARTIST achieves only 36.63% vs. TimeMaster+RL's 72.55% (36-point gap), suggesting approach may fail on biomedical signals; this critical finding receives insufficient analysis
Limited technical scope: restricted to univariate time series, contiguous segments only (no multi-span), and max 3 segment selections; constraint justifications not provided

Inference cost not quantified: paper acknowledges 'additional inference cost' but provides no latency measurements, number of typical segment selections, or cost-benefit analysis critical for practitioners
Hyperparameter choices unjustified: controller/reasoner temperatures (1.0/0.7), LoRA rank, learning rate (1×10⁻⁶) lack ablations or justification
Reliability reward dependency on LLM stochasticity: approach critically depends on temperature-based variance (Eq. 8); generalization to deterministic models or different architectures unexplored
Missing statistical significance testing: while 8 runs reported, no confidence intervals or tests; is 6.46% improvement statistically robust?
Insufficient error analysis: no breakdown of which question types benefit from adaptive selection, failure mode analysis beyond one example, or investigation of anomalous results

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying a genuine gap in time series reasoning: most prior work encodes full series upfront despite question-dependent segment relevance
Solid technical approach with controller-reasoner decomposition that meaningfully separates segment selection from reasoning, plus hierarchical RL with appropriate credit assignment across rounds
Clever use of reliability rewards (Eq. 8) to handle LLM stochasticity via consistency across rollouts, and variance-guided sampling (Eq. 12) for informative segment prioritization
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks with strong empirical results: 6.46% average accuracy improvement with up to 12.5% gains on rare event/multi-segment tasks
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of key components: adaptive selection (-9.30%), reliability reward (-21.44%), hierarchical optimization (-12.28%)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, training costs, dataset descriptions, and supplementary analyses of data utilization patterns and long-sequence generalization
Well-written paper with clear motivation, accessible technical presentation, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Substantial inference cost of 1.6-2.1× per example compared to baselines (Table 8) is relegated to Appendix I despite being a significant practical limitation for deployment
Inconsistent performance across datasets: Sleep-QA (36.63%) substantially underperforms TimeMaster+RL (72.55%), indicating modality/representation sensitivities not fully addressed in main approach

Limited technical novelty—builds incrementally on recent self-play RL work (AZR, SPICE, SPELL); controller-reasoner decomposition is sensible but not novel; reliability rewards are straightforward accuracy averaging

Evaluation fairness concerns: uneven SFT treatment across baselines, no statistical significance tests, some improvements modest (1-3%) without confidence intervals, comparison sometimes mixes method and representation effects

Restricted scope: univariate only, most benchmarks are short (22-4,000 tokens), long-sequence experiments use artificial setup (tiling + noise rather than realistic long series), no multivariate evaluation

SFT data introduces circularity: GPT-5 creates gold standard traces then ARTIST fine-tunes on them; ablation shows SFT gain (+5.65%) substantially exceeds RL gain (+0.81%), raising attribution questions

Design choices under-justified: different controller/reasoner temperatures (1.0 vs 0.7) mentioned only in appendix, format reward penalties appear ad-hoc, missing ablations on format rewards and interaction round limits

Incomplete analysis: only 3 qualitative examples (Figure 4), no systematic study of failure modes, missing analysis of how questions yield different segment selections, limited comparison with PixelReasoner (Table 7, single dataset)
